* **The Bullet in the Wall:** The lab features a specialized **water shoot tank**. Detectives will recover his gun, fire a test round into the water tank to catch a pristine bullet, and use a comparison microscope to match the microscopic scratches (striations) from the barrel to the bullet dug out of the drywall.

Your late-bloomer character, isolated at home with his mom during lockdowns, would have spent his evenings deeply hyper-fixating on obscure internet forums, reading these exact newly released forensic papers. Here is how you fix his knowledge level, refine your dialogue, and answer your scientific question about the ice age reset.

Make Leo a **gullible recorder**. He has all this dire information, but he doesn't fully understand the weight of it, and he actually thinks some of it might be a lie or an internet prank.

* **Why he refused to join the mission:** He didn't join because he thought Marcus and the others were completely insane or part of a weird doomsday cult. Even after seeing the "weird blood" and the shootout, his simple-minded brain rationalized it away as a high-tech gang war or a drug hallucination. He stayed behind because staying with his mom was safe, familiar, and real—while space travel sounded like a crazy sci-fi movie he didn't want to be in.  
* **The "I'm Just the Delivery Guy" Defense:** When the detectives press him, he admits he only knows this because he was sitting on Marcus's living room couch waiting for his drug payout while Marcus was screaming at an invisible wall (or a cloaked alien communicator).

2\. Tightening Your Dialogue (Punchy & Realistic)

By making the dialogue shorter and show his lack of understanding, it sounds much more natural for a scared, simple-minded kid in a 2020 interrogation room.

**Leo:** (Leaning forward, voice low) *"I'm telling you, man. I'm not lying. They're everywhere. They change how they look. Some look just like you and me. Marcus was screaming at one in the kitchen right before the glass broke."*

**Lead Detective:** *"Who is 'they', Leo? The people you kidnapped?"*

**Leo:** *"The governments. All of them. Marcus said they’re working together on bases and spaceships. They’re getting ready to leave Earth, and they aren't taking everybody with them. They tried population control, but it failed. Marcus said they're just waiting for a rock to hit us now. An asteroid. They have underground cities ready. They'll survive. We won't. We don't have anywhere to hide."*

**Second Detective:** *"Bunkers. Some people have bunkers."*

**Leo:** *"Yeah, well, Marcus said some people might survive the impact, but nobody can live in a hole in the dirt for a hundred years while the surface freezes over."*

**Lead Detective:** *"And you believed this guy?"*

**Leo:** (Shrugging, completely sincere) *"I thought he was smoking something, honestly. I just wanted my money so I could buy some new shoes and help my mom with rent. Why would I go to space with a bunch of lunatics? I like it here."*

3\. The Science: Could a New Ice Age Affect Only Certain Places?

To answer your research question: **Yes, absolutely.** If an asteroid impacts Earth or a massive global cataclysm triggers a "reset," a new ice age would not freeze the entire planet equally.

* **The Impact Winter:** An asteroid strike throws millions of tons of dust and ash into the stratosphere, blocking out the sun. This triggers an "Impact Winter" that can last for decades.  
* **The Equatorial Shield:** The worst of the ice age would hit the Northern and Southern hemispheres (freezing North America, Europe, and Asia under miles of ice). However, the **equatorial regions** (Central America, parts of Africa, and Northern South America) would remain clear of solid ice sheets. They would become incredibly dark, cold, and rainy, but the ground wouldn't be buried in glaciers.  
* **The 100-Year Timeline:** A severe impact winter takes about 10 to 30 years for the heavy dust to fully settle, but the resulting alteration of ocean currents and destroyed ecosystems could easily keep the planet in a brutal, unlivable deep-freeze for **100 to 200 years** before the atmosphere stabilizes.

Why This Fix Makes the Scene Brilliant

It perfectly balances his character. Leo has the absolute, terrifying blueprints to the end of the world, but because he is a simple, late-blooming warehouse worker, he treated the most important information in human history like "crazy talk" from a bad drug client. He chose a brand-new Honda Civic over saving his own life, which makes his eventual forced transformation at the end of your story incredibly tragic.

For a 30-year veteran detective, **Scorpio** is the ultimate sign.

* **How it fits:** A Scorpio detective won’t care that the government deleted the file or that it's been six years. The obsession keeps him up at night. He will dig until he finds the truth, even if it destroys his peace of mind.

* **His Usual Cases:** He spent his career in **Homicide and Missing Persons**. He is used to dealing with the worst days of people's lives—cluttered crime scenes, grieving parents, and cold trails.  
* **His Most Challenging Case:** The **"Marcus and Leo" case in 2020**. Before this, he thought he had seen every way a human could hurt another human. This case shattered his understanding of reality because the evidence didn't obey the laws of physics or forensics.  
* **His Biggest Letdown (Common among detectives):** The crushing realization that **the justice system doesn't care about the truth, only closure.** It is incredibly common for detectives to watch a clear-cut case fall apart because of a legal technicality, administrative laziness, or political pressure. * **What he Hated Most about the Job:** **The Bureaucracy and Politics.** He hated the "suits" from Uptown Charlotte and federal alphabet agencies who swooped in to take credit for wins but buried the messy, unexplained failures to keep the city's public image clean.

3\. The Promise and The Partner Dynamic

* **The Broken Promise:** Yes, he sat in the living room of Marcus’s parents in early 2020 and looked them in the eye. He gave them the ultimate taboo promise in police work: *"I am going to bring your boy home."* Breaking that promise is a rot that eats at his soul every day.  
* **The Relationship with the Lead Detective:** He didn't resent his partner; **he loved him like a brother.** His partner was a sharp, traditional, old-school cop. When his partner died of COVID-19 in 2020, it devastated him. He feels an intense, heavy survivor's guilt.  
* **The Tribute:** He works this case in his spare time in 2026 as a strict **dual tribute**. He owes it to Marcus’s grieving family, but he also owes it to his dead partner. He refuses to let his partner’s final case remain an unsolved, deleted joke in a precinct archive.

4\. His Evolution into a UFO Investigator

* **His Initial Skepticism:** He was a hardcore, cynical skeptic before 2020\. He used to laugh at people who talked about aliens, grouping them with the junkies and mentally ill people he encountered on the streets of Charlotte.

He applies his 30 years of real police interrogation tactics and evidence-gathering techniques to alien sightings, filtering out the hoaxes to find the hard data.

5\. What He Found in the Government Leaks

Since his retirement, he has spent years combing through the recently released, unclassified UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena) documents. He finally found his "smoking gun":

* **The Video Evidence:** Hidden inside an unclassified 2024 Department of Defense data drop—hidden under a boring file name like *“Atmospheric Anomaly Test Closeout”*—he found a short, grainy thermal drone clip.

The narrative friction here is that Austin is simultaneously hunting Lou while preparing for a space mission. To fix this cleanly, **we must eliminate Austin’s physical knocking on Lou's door.**

Instead, Austin is leaving those physical tracks (like the sticky notes and cash offers) **prior to his official abduction/recruitment**, or a shadow military operative is planting those notes using Austin's name to see if Lou has the container.

By streamlining the sequence where Lou and Dyon open the cylinder with the junkie "Moot," we maintain a grounded pacing. It portrays Lou as a desperate, small-time hustler completely out of his depth.

\[0:00 \- 1:30\] SECTION 1: THE DISCONTINUED FILE

**(Tone: Cold, steady, leaning into the microphone)**

\*\*NARRATOR:\*\*Six years ago, during the first wave of the pandemic, if you told people you saw a gray entity in a dining room in East Charlotte, the CMPD locked you in a psych holding cell.

Today? The government releases hundreds of unclassified UFO documents, video of objects shot down over the Middle East, and people just scroll past it on their phones to watch a dance trend. We’re too distracted to care.

The brass told me our 2020 file on the missing Marcus kid and the warehouse worker, Lou Jackson, was accidentally purged during a routine server migration. That’s code for a federal vacuum. If you search the database for Lou’s name, or the bullet we pulled out of that drywall on East Trade Street, you get a "File Not Found" error.

I know because I check every single month.

I was sitting in my living room recently, watching an episode of *The Why Files* on YouTube. The host was doing a deep dive on black-budget spacecraft and engineered population resets. Suddenly, I felt the hair on my arms stand up. He quoted an old, obscure leak about an impending "Impact Winter"—a climate reset designed to clean out the surface populace.

It was almost word-for-word what that twenty-three-year-old kid, Lou, mumbled into my tape recorder before he vanished. *The Why Files* thought it was just a compelling conspiracy theory.

But I sat there in the dark knowing it was real. Because I’m the old-school detective who still has the ruined micro-cassette to prove it.

\[1:30 \- 4:15\] SECTION 2: THE JEDI AND THE HUSTLER

**(Tone: Narrative, painting the picture of the characters)**

\*\*NARRATOR:\*\*The case started on Saturday night, October twenty-fourth, 2020\. At exactly eleven-fifteen p.m., a couple on Charlotte's East side received a bizarre phone call from a strange number. It was their son, Austin Frye.

Austin was a twenty-three-year-old EMT. A total "square." The hardest thing he ever drank was a Sprite. He was completely obsessed with *Star Wars*, practiced tai chi, and spent his nights meditating, looking for what he called his "higher purpose."

On the phone, Austin sounded completely cold. He told his folks he was leaving for India immediately to volunteer at a Covid clinic. He couldn't name the town. He wasn't coming home to pack. Before they could ask about his brand-new Toyota Camry, he hung up. The parents tried calling back, but it just spat a busy signal. No voicemail. Nothing.

The CMPD didn't give a damn at first. They thought the kid cracked under pandemic stress and ran off with his secret college girlfriend, Kayla.

But the timeline didn't fit. We pulled the GPS logs from Austin’s new Camry. It put the car miles away from his parents, idling outside the house of a small-time weed dealer named Louis "Trip" Jackson.

Lou was the polar opposite of Austin. A high school dropout who got his GED just to stop his mama from fussing. Six feet tall, slim, always rocking a doo-rag and a flashing chain with his personal brand logo. Lou wanted to be a rap mogul like Rick Ross or Master P. He cussed constantly and treated street thugs and police detectives with the exact same casual disrespect.

When my partner and I pulled Lou into the box on a grand theft auto charge, he tried to play the tough-guy entrepreneur. But when we threatened him with a federal triple-homicide indictment, his entire hustle evaporated. He made us swear on our children’s lives that we weren't working for the CIA, the FBI, or "hybrid-human aliens."

Then he told us about October thirteenth behind the Home Depot on Wendover Road.

\[4:15 \- 7:00\] SECTION 3: THE DIAMOND SALT

**(Tone: Shifting into pure, unsettling sci-fi reality)**

\*\*NARRATOR:\*\*Lou told us he got off a city bus at ten-fifteen p.m. to buy beer, taking a shortcut across the train tracks behind the Home Depot. Suddenly, he heard taser-like popping sounds and saw flashes of light near the homeless camp by the bridge privacy fence.

Then he saw a man leap completely over a six-foot fence in a single bound, toss a flashing device that left people screaming in agony on the other side, and crash into the bushes. Lou dives behind a stack of mulch. The next second, a deafening hum vibrates straight through his bones, a sharp pain spikes his skull, and a low-flying, cloaked craft buzzes the parking lot so hard Lou passes out in the dirt, soaking his hoodie in spilled beer.

When Lou woke up, the jumper was gone. But lying in the grass was a dark metallic cylinder.

Lou and his handy-man buddy Dyon used a commercial bench vice to crack the seals. Inside sat a pristine bed of white and blue crystals that sparkled like crushed diamonds. Lou sniffed it. It was completely odorless. To test it, they literally fed a sample to a local street user named Moot in the back of a parked sedan. Moot tasted it, said it tasted like sweet licorice, and sat there completely sober for an hour. Moot told them it was probably just dummy chemical junk for a pandemic vaccine.

Lou thought he was holding trash. He didn't realize that the crystals were completely dormant because they were missing the final catalyst: human adrenaline.

Austin Frye was the EMT on the call that picked up the burned man from the tracks. Austin figured out what Lou had. He tracked Lou down through the dispatch logs, left a sticky note on his door offering a two-hundred-and-fifty-dollar bribe, and eventually forced a meeting.

By Friday, Lou sold Austin a forty-gram sample in a plastic sandwich bag for two thousand dollars cash. Lou thought he was a king pin. He had no idea Austin was taking that sample to his financier—a fifty-three-year-old retired mail carrier named Doc who lived off Pineville-Matthews Road.

\[7:00 \- 9:30\] SECTION 4: THE RESETS AND THE SHOCK-TROOPS

**(Tone: Deeply paranoid, uncovering the cosmic lore)**

\*\*NARRATOR:\*\*During the interrogation, Lou summarized what Austin told him during a desperate twenty-minute phone call. Austin had already ingested the pure formula after consulting with a black-budget scientist. Lou said Austin was physically changing before his eyes—growing taller, heavily muscled, his face bolder, walking with a terrifying supernatural pep.

Austin told Lou the truth about the formula. It wasn't a narcotic. It was an interstellar stabilizer required to survive an automated eight-year hibernation transit on spacecraft managed entirely by artificial intelligence systems.

Austin dropped the entire cosmic map on him. Seventy years ago, a non-hostile alien faction mapped out a hyper-nutritional target planet called Teo 7 for humanity. The unique planetary vegetation behaves like a biological catalyst—mutating human DNA back to its purest, ancient form, accelerating muscle synthesis and consciousness until humans become supernatural.

But it triggered a galactic civil war. A hostile hybrid faction—the Nephilim—hates Earthlings. They view us as primitive descendants of ancient Reptilians who polluted the planet after the Great Flood. They don't want humans inheriting Teo 7\.

And the world governments? They’ve known about the 2030 surface catastrophe for decades. They’re actively building underground cities and fueling exodus ships for the elite—scientists, engineers, and politicians. They view the upcoming surface depopulation as a logistical blessing. They even deploy "gangstalkers" to harass the homeless because they're terrified that unhoused people and off-grid preppers actually have the survival skills to live through the freeze and disrupt the reset.

Austin offered Lou and his family a guaranteed manifest on the ships. But Lou refused. Lou told us: *"Austin is crazy, man. He’s gonna end up looking like one of them gray hybrid monsters. I didn't want to turn into no alien. I just wanted to take my money, buy a nice car, and enjoy whatever time I got left on this dirt."*

Lou didn't care about the universe. He hung up on a space prophet because he had a date waiting in his driveway.

\[9:30 \- END\] SECTION 5: THE EVACUATION

**(Tone: Heavy, dramatic finish, slowing down the pace)**

\*\*NARRATOR:\*\*The final transaction was set for Sunday afternoon, October twenty-fifth, at Doc’s house. Doc didn't care about human currency—he was a detached, neutral observer. He stuffed a secret one hundred thousand dollars into a black tote bag for Lou just because he saw the kid loved money. Lou stashed seventy grand behind his closet baseboards and told everyone he only got forty.

But before the cash could change hands, the garage door exploded.

Three Nephilim hybrid assassins breached the room. Lou reached for his illegal strap, but a kinetic projectile shattered his bicep, sending his gun flying. While Doc cleared the floor in a single flying kick, Austin went completely berserker with a heavy iron fireplace poker, beating the remaining two hitters to death in a thirty-second bloodbath.

They loaded the three non-human corpses into the back of Doc's twenty-fourteen Chevy Tahoe. Austin, bleeding from a chest wound that was already miraculously regenerating, handed Lou the keys to his Camry for keeps. They executed a vehicle swap on Independence Boulevard and vanished into the night.

We had to let Lou go. The forensic team found the bullet in the drywall, the long brown hair belonging to Kayla, and Dyon's bare fingerprint on the outside doorknob. But with no bodies and pandemic-shortened scheduling, we couldn't hold them. We set up surveillance, waiting for Lou to lead us to Austin.

But the universe broke Lou anyway.

On Thanksgiving, his mama caught the virus. By December twenty-second, she was dead. On Christmas Eve, his little brother’s biological dad stripped the kid of his necessities and drove away, leaving Lou entirely alone in an empty house on Christmas Day. In January, he was laid off from his warehouse job. The police department refused to return his seized cash.

On January eighth, his relatives swarmed the house like vultures, stripping his mama’s remaining belongings. Lou sat in the dark with seventy thousand dollars of hidden alien cash that couldn't buy back a single thing that mattered.

A week later, his cousin unlocked the front door with a spare key. The house was a wreck. Lou was completely gone. His mama’s car was found abandoned on a side street. Lou never made it to his second interrogation.

Most people look at the skies today, watching military leaks and billionaire rocket launches, wondering when the aliens are going to arrive.

They’ve got the whole dynamic backward. The timeline is running out, the automated colony ships are warming their engines in the underground hangars, and the elites have already signed the manifests.

This isn't a story about an invasion. This is the logbook of an evacuation.

And now you finally know the truth... behind why the aliens left Earth.
